video.title: Inference, Diffusion, World Models, and More | YC Paper Club
video.display_title_html: Inference, Diffusion, World Models, and More | YC Paper Club

thesis: Five researchers walk through frontier papers showing that the next gains in AI come less from bigger pretraining and more from rethinking the stack — parallelizing inference for capability, factorized diffusion world models for control, elegant anti-collapse regularizers, classical generalization theory, and trading infinite compute for scarce data.

chapters.title: Intro from YC Visiting Partner Francois Chaubard
Akshay Vegesna — Deep Learning is Not So Mysterious or Different
Konwoo Kim — Pretraining Under Infinite Compute

insights.headline: Inference speed is the new ceiling on intelligence
insights.body: Tanishq Kumar argues inference is treated as a cost/convenience lever, but within 1-3 years it becomes a capability: if a method's performance scales with how much it thinks, then tokens-per-second is literally the peak intelligence you can deliver. He frames the goal as a datacenter of 20,000 B200s working on the Riemann hypothesis.

insights.headline: RL now exceeds pretraining's compute demands
insights.body: Kumar notes that not only do inference costs dominate training when serving billions of users (trillions of tokens), but within training, RL is starting to exceed the compute requirements of pretraining — and RL is itself just a wrapper on inference.

insights.headline: Speculative decoding works because verifying beats generating
insights.body: A small draft model autoregressively guesses tokens; the big target model verifies them in a single parallel forward pass and accepts those it would plausibly have generated. The key asymmetry is a transformer feature: you can score many tokens in parallel but can only generate one at a time.

insights.headline: SSD parallelizes drafting and verification across hardware
insights.body: Speculative Speculative Decoding breaks the sequential dependency by having the draft model anticipate the most likely verification outcomes and start drafting the next round on separate hardware while the big model verifies — hiding drafting latency entirely. It predicts verification outcomes correctly 80-90% of the time using the draft's own unsampled token distributions.

insights.headline: SSD hits 300 tokens/sec on Llama 70B, 4xH100
insights.body: Kumar's hand-rolled inference engine running SSD beats SGLang (the fastest engine they tested with speculative decoding) and wins on both latency and throughput — sampling Llama 3 70B at 300 tokens/second on four H100s.

insights.headline: Diffusion-MPC factorizes action proposal from dynamics
insights.body: Stannis Zhou's Diffusion-MPC uses diffusion models to learn multi-step action proposals and multi-step dynamics separately. Because the dynamics model is factored out, when a walker's left ankle 'breaks,' you can adapt only the dynamics model on a little play data and recover performance — something joint-modeling approaches can't do.

insights.headline: Stronger models let you simplify the planner
insights.body: Zhou found empirically that using diffusion models — powerful multi-modal data modelers — for both proposals and dynamics let them replace complex planning with a very simple sampling-based planner and still outperform prior state-of-the-art.

insights.headline: World models are a 1990 idea in new packaging
insights.body: Isaac Ward traces 'world models' back to a NeurIPS 1990 paper — older than the average attendee — and to Richard Sutton's exact description of a black box that takes situation plus action and outputs the next situation. The label is new advertising on an old idea, now backed by Yann LeCun's $1.03B March raise.

insights.headline: SIGREG: keep latents Gaussian to avoid collapse
insights.body: Lay World Model's contribution is a single regularizer — Sketched Isotropic Gaussian regularization — that takes 1D slices over high-dimensional embeddings and forces each to be Gaussian distributed, cheaply enforcing a healthy non-collapsed latent space with one loss term and one hyperparameter instead of elaborate tricks.

insights.headline: World models can quantify their own surprise
insights.body: When Ward's team teleports or recolors the T in a push-T task, the world model's prediction error spikes detectably at the exact moment of perturbation — giving model-based agents uncertainty estimates that model-free policies don't natively provide. Lay World Model also runs 50x faster than competitors on under 24GB VRAM with just 15M parameters.

insights.headline: Generalization isn't a mystery — it's PAC-Bayes
insights.body: Akshay Vegesna presents Andrew Gordon Wilson's argument that overparameterization, benign overfitting, and double descent are explained by classical PAC-Bayes bounds (training loss plus a compression term). Bigger models find flatter minima, whose volume grows exponentially with parameters, and flat minima are more compressible — yielding non-vacuous generalization bounds even at billion-parameter scale.

insights.headline: Ensembles beat one big model when data-constrained
insights.body: Konwoo Kim shows that under fixed data, training a 5-ensemble of small models beats training a single compute-matched large model. Both regularization (weight decay ~30x larger than compute-optimal) and ensembling yield clean power laws with measurable asymptotes; standard recipes overfit and have no asymptote at all.

insights.headline: Joint scaling buys a 5x data-efficiency win
insights.body: Kim's joint regularization-plus-ensembling recipe yields roughly 5x effective data efficiency over the standard recipe, projected to hold even at 10 trillion seed tokens. An 8-ensemble can be distilled into a single 300M model retaining ~83% of the gain, and on continued pretraining, 4B math tokens match training on the full 73B (a 17x win).

insights.headline: Self-distillation beats the regularized asymptote
insights.body: Kim shows distilling a 300M model into a fresh 300M model improves loss and even beats the asymptote of the regularized recipe — counterintuitive, but connected to prior work viewing self-distillation as implicitly training a two-member ensemble.

action_items: If you take one thing: treat inference speed as a capability lever, not just a cost — methods whose performance scales with thinking make tokens/sec the real intelligence ceiling.
When data-constrained but compute-rich, abandon the single-big-model instinct: combine aggressive regularization with ensembling, then distill back down for cheap inference.
Factorize action proposal from dynamics in robotics control so you can adapt to changed dynamics with a little play data instead of retraining everything.
Stop calling generalization a mystery — reach for classical PAC-Bayes and soft inductive biases before inventing new explanations.
